**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Thursday

---

Over the past few weeks we've been circling a decision that deserves to be settled properly rather than drifted into: whether we should purchase additional local AI hardware, or invest the next quarter in raising the utilisation of the machines we already own. I want to lay out how I see the trade-offs, make a recommendation, and be honest about where my confidence runs out.

The starting point is that our current fleet is not obviously overloaded. Across the last eight weeks, our inference nodes have averaged somewhere between 35 and 45 percent utilisation, with bursts into the high eighties during batch jobs and long idle stretches overnight and at weekends. Training runs are scheduled around availability rather than demand, which is a symptom worth taking seriously, but the day-to-day picture is one of a fleet that is busy in patches and quiet in between. Buying more hardware against that profile would mean paying for capacity we already possess but fail to schedule well. Capital cost is only the visible part of that. There is also rack space, power, cooling, and — the cost we most often forget — the engineering time to install, integrate, monitor, and eventually decommission the new kit. Every hour someone spends racking a new node is an hour not spent on the product work that actually justifies our existence.

Latency is the strongest argument on the buying side, and I want to acknowledge it rather than wave it away. Our interactive workloads do suffer when a training job hogs the cluster, and p95 response times degrade in ways users notice. But the right first response to contention is not necessarily more capacity; it is better isolation. Queueing discipline, workload partitioning, and sensible preemption would address most of the latency pain at a fraction of the cost of new hardware. If, after those changes, latency still fails to meet our targets at acceptable utilisation levels, that would be genuine evidence of a capacity shortfall — and we'd be in a much stronger position to size the purchase correctly, because we'd finally know our true demand curve rather than the distorted one produced by today's scheduling chaos.

Reliability cuts both ways. A larger fleet gives us redundancy, and I don't want to pretend otherwise; right now a failure on node three takes a meaningful slice of our throughput with it. But reliability is also a function of operational maturity, and a modest fleet that is well-monitored, well-maintained, and not running at 95 percent saturation is often more dependable in practice than a larger one run hot by a team that hasn't had time to build proper failover. Utilisation work — better telemetry, graceful draining, automated recovery — improves reliability directly. New hardware improves it only indirectly, and only if we also do the operational work, which we would then have less time for.

The opportunity-cost question is the one I keep returning to. The budget for a serious hardware purchase would fund roughly two engineer-quarters. Spent on utilisation, that buys scheduling improvements, capacity modelling, and the measurement infrastructure we conspicuously lack. Spent on metal, it buys machines whose value depends on assumptions about our workload growth that we have not validated. And there is the reversibility asymmetry, which I think is decisive. Utilisation work is almost entirely reversible: if we build a better scheduler and it turns out we didn't need it, we've lost little and learned a great deal about our demand. Hardware is not reversible in any comfortable sense. It depreciates, it consumes power whether we use it or not, and unwinding a purchase means writing off sunk cost in full view of everyone who asked why we bought it.

So my recommendation is this: commit the next quarter to utilisation and scheduling work, with explicit, pre-agreed thresholds. If, by the end of that period, we are sustaining utilisation above roughly 70 percent while still missing our latency targets, or if demand growth makes the shortfall unambiguous, we proceed to a hardware purchase with real data behind it. I want to be clear that this is a recommendation made under uncertainty, not a certainty dressed up as one. My utilisation figures come from partial telemetry, and it's possible that the quiet stretches are quieter in aggregate than our sampling suggests, or that the bursty demand we see is itself suppressed by current constraints — people don't submit jobs they've learned the cluster can't handle. That second possibility is the one that most genuinely worries me, and it's why the measurement work comes first: it is precisely the tool for finding out whether I'm wrong.

If anyone disagrees, particularly those closest to the day-to-day contention problems, I'd genuinely like to hear it before we commit. Let's discuss at Monday's planning session.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Thursday

We've reached the point in the quarter where the queue for our inference cluster has become visible enough that people are asking what we're going to do about it. The instinctive answer — buy more hardware — is understandable, and I want to take it seriously rather than dismiss it. But I've spent the last week looking at our utilisation numbers, and I think the honest conclusion is that we don't yet have a capacity problem. We have an allocation problem, and the two look identical from the outside while costing very different amounts to fix.

Start with the numbers. Across the last thirty days, our eight A100s averaged 41% utilisation, with a peak-to-trough spread that would be comical if it weren't costing us money. Monday mornings the cluster saturates and jobs queue for hours; Friday afternoons it idles. The batch training pipeline hogs four cards whether or not it needs them, because someone set a static reservation eight months ago and nobody has had the political energy to unclaim it. Our fine-tuning experiments run at full precision when quantised versions would fit comfortably on half the memory. None of this is anyone's fault in particular — it's the natural sediment that accumulates when a small team is moving fast and hardware is shared informally. But it means that before we spend several hundred thousand dollars on new cards, we should be confident we're buying capacity and not just buying our way around bad scheduling.

The cost case for buying is not trivial, and it's not just the purchase price. There's power, cooling, rack space, and the operational tax of more machines to patch and monitor. There's also depreciation: this generation of accelerators loses value quickly, and whatever we buy now will be worth a fraction of its cost in three years. Against that, the cost of improving utilisation is mostly time — a proper scheduler, dynamic allocation instead of static reservations, maybe a lightweight internal quota system. I'd estimate two to three engineer-weeks. That's real, and it's time we'd otherwise spend on product work, which is exactly the opportunity cost we should be weighing. But two engineer-weeks against a six-figure capital outlay is a trade I'm comfortable making, at least once.

Latency is the strongest argument on the buying side, and I want to acknowledge it properly. Interactive work — the demo notebooks, the customer-facing prototype, the on-call debugging session — genuinely suffers when the cluster is saturated. Queuing delays of forty minutes are not an acceptable experience for someone trying to close a deal. If better scheduling shaved the average wait but left the Monday-morning spike intact, we'd still have a problem. My answer to this is that scheduling improvements and a small amount of reserved headroom can address the spike more cheaply than new hardware can. If we formalise a priority tier — say, two cards reserved for interactive work, with batch jobs preemptible — we protect the experience that matters without doubling our fleet. Preemption for batch jobs is annoying but tolerable; checkpointing is a solved problem and our training runs are already fault-tolerant.

Reliability cuts both ways. More machines means more redundancy, and right now a single node failure takes out half our training capacity. That's a legitimate fragility. But redundancy bought on top of 41% utilisation is redundancy we're paying to keep idle, and I'd rather first make the existing fleet resilient — better health checks, automatic job recovery, a documented failover path — and see whether the residual risk justifies capital.

There's also the question of reversibility, which I think is decisive. Buying hardware is a one-way door. Once the purchase order is signed, the money is spent, the depreciation clock is running, and we own the maintenance burden regardless of whether our demand forecast was right. Improving utilisation is a two-way door: if we build the scheduler, fix the reservations, and find that demand still exceeds capacity, we've lost a few weeks and gained permanent operational discipline that we'd want anyway. The information we gain from trying the cheap option first makes the expensive option, if we eventually take it, better targeted — we'll know our true baseline demand rather than our demand-plus-waste.

So my recommendation is this: we spend the next month on utilisation. Dynamic scheduling, preemption, a priority tier for interactive work, and a weekly utilisation report so this stops being invisible. We revisit the purchase decision at the end of that month with real numbers. If sustained demand above 75% utilisation persists for two consecutive weeks, I'll write the capital request myself and advocate for it enthusiastically.

I want to be clear about the uncertainty here, because I don't want anyone to read this as a promise that we won't need to buy hardware. Demand is growing, and it's genuinely possible that a month from now the answer is obvious in the other direction. What I'm arguing against is buying now, on the basis of a number that I believe understates our effective capacity by a factor of two. If I'm wrong about that — if the waste is less than I think, or the scheduler takes longer than estimated — we'll have spent a month and learned it definitively. That's a cheap mistake. Buying eight GPUs we didn't need is not.

Comments welcome, especially from anyone who's lived through a preemption-based setup and can tell me where it hurts. I'd rather hear the objections now than discover them in production.

— J.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Local AI hardware investment decision
**Status:** For discussion ahead of Thursday's planning session

We've reached the point where our local inference cluster is saturated during peak hours, and the question on the table is whether we should purchase additional hardware or invest in squeezing more out of what we already own. I want to lay out my thinking before we meet, because I believe the answer is more one-sided than our recent conversations have suggested.

The case for buying more hardware is easy to state: we have real demand we can't currently serve, and GPUs are the direct remedy. But that framing hides the actual economics. Our current fleet runs at roughly 40% average utilisation, with peaks that hit 95% and troughs that fall below 15%. That profile is not a capacity problem in any simple sense — it is a scheduling and batching problem. The hardware we need to serve tomorrow's peak already exists in our racks; it is simply idle at the wrong hours and under-batched at the busy ones. Buying more machines to solve this would mean paying full price for capacity that duplicates what we own, while the underlying inefficiency persists and compounds as we grow.

The cost asymmetry matters here. Capital purchases are front-loaded, irreversible in practice — resale value on specialised accelerators is poor and depreciation is fast — and they carry ongoing costs in power, cooling, rack space, and the operational attention of a team that is already stretched thin. The alternative path, improving utilisation, is mostly an investment of engineering time: continuous batching, better request routing, quantisation where quality trade-offs are acceptable, off-peak scheduling of batch jobs, and a proper queueing layer so that interactive traffic and background workloads stop competing for the same memory at the same moments. That work is cheap relative to hardware, it compounds — every improvement applies to every future workload — and, crucially, it is reversible. If we invest three engineer-months in utilisation work and it turns out the demand curve has shifted underneath us, we've lost time but gained a permanently better-scheduled cluster. If we buy hardware and demand doesn't materialise, we've lost capital we cannot get back.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side, and I want to take it seriously. Our interactive workloads have p95 latency targets, and right now we breach them during peak windows. More hardware would fix that immediately. But the latency we're seeing is largely queueing latency, not compute latency — requests are waiting for batches to fill and for memory to free up, not being processed slowly. Queueing latency is exactly what utilisation work addresses. There is genuine uncertainty about how much of our p95 problem is queueing versus raw throughput, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. My proposal includes a measurement phase precisely because of that: two weeks of instrumented profiling will tell us what fraction of tail latency is recoverable through scheduling. If the answer is "less than half," the case for hardware strengthens considerably, and we should revisit this with better data.

There is also an opportunity cost to weigh on both sides. The engineers who would do the utilisation work are the same ones we'd need to integrate and operate new hardware. Buying machines doesn't save their time; it redirects it toward procurement, capacity planning, and vendor management — work that produces no reusable capability. The utilisation path, by contrast, produces skills and infrastructure (a real scheduler, better observability, batching infrastructure) that we will need regardless of how much hardware we eventually own. In effect, the utilisation investment is a prerequisite for any future hardware purchase being efficient, so it is not time lost even in the world where we end up buying.

My recommendation, then: defer the hardware purchase for one quarter. Spend the next two weeks on profiling to establish where latency actually comes from, then six to eight weeks on batching, scheduling, and queueing improvements. Set explicit success criteria now — if peak-hour p95 latency meets target and utilisation rises above 65%, we hold off on purchase; if we fall materially short, we bring a hardware request back to this group with profiling data in hand, and I suspect it will be approved quickly and rightly.

The honest summary is this: we are not yet in a position to know whether we need more hardware, because we have never operated our existing hardware well enough to find out. Buying now would be paying to avoid answering a question we can answer cheaply. Let's answer it first.

I'm happy to walk through the utilisation numbers with anyone before Thursday.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Buy more GPU hardware, or get more out of what we have?
**Date:** Thursday

**Summary and recommendation**

We've been debating for two weeks whether to purchase additional local inference hardware or to invest the same effort in raising utilisation of the four accelerators we already own. My recommendation is that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation first, and defer any purchase decision until we have hard numbers from that effort. This is not a permanent "no" to buying hardware; it is a deliberate sequencing decision, and I want to explain why I think it is the right one even though the case for buying is not crazy.

**Where we actually stand**

Our current fleet sits at roughly 30–35% utilisation by wall-clock measurement, with peaks near 90% during batch windows and long idle stretches overnight and on weekends. That profile is the strongest argument against buying more capacity right now. Every additional card we purchase would, on current scheduling, spend most of its life doing nothing, while depreciating, consuming power, occupying rack space, and adding another unit to maintain. The marginal cost of capacity is not just the sticker price; it is the operating burden and the attention of a team that is already stretched thin.

The counterargument, and it is a fair one, is latency. Our interactive workloads suffer during peak windows, and a couple of people have reasonably said that queuing behind batch jobs is a poor experience that no amount of clever scheduling fully fixes. There is truth in that. But when I look at the actual contention events, most of them trace back to jobs that could run at a lower priority, to models held resident in memory when nobody is using them, or to batch windows scheduled at times that collide with peak interactive demand rather than avoiding it. Those are utilisation and scheduling problems wearing a capacity-problem costume.

**Cost and opportunity cost**

The capital cost of a meaningful hardware addition would be substantial relative to our budget, and it is worth being honest about what else that money could do. The same funds could cover a contractor to build proper queueing and autoscaling logic, better observability into per-job resource use, or a second engineer-month on the reliability work we keep deferring. If we buy hardware and it turns out the bottleneck was scheduling all along, we will have spent our one big lever of the year on the wrong thing. Opportunity cost is invisible when you spend well and obvious when you don't, which is exactly why it deserves explicit thought now.

There is also a running-cost asymmetry. Utilisation work costs mostly engineering time, which is renewable and partially reversible; hardware costs capital and floor space, which are not. Once a card is on the shelf, the incentive to justify it quietly warps our planning. I would rather not create that pressure.

**Reliability and reversibility**

Reliability cuts both ways, and I want to acknowledge that. More hardware gives us redundancy: if a card fails today, we lose a third of our capacity, and that is a genuine risk. Utilisation improvements do nothing for fault tolerance, and pushing existing hardware harder may even accelerate wear or expose thermal issues. This is the strongest argument on the buy side, and I don't want to minimise it. But redundancy can be bought later, once we know our true steady-state need, and buying it later costs roughly the same as buying it now. The reverse is not true: if we buy now and the need never materialises, the money is gone.

Reversibility favours the same path. Scheduling changes, memory-pooling, and better batching are all adjustable or undoable. A purchase is a one-way door in practice, given our procurement cycle and the resale value of used accelerators. When one option preserves optionality and the other spends it, and we are this uncertain about the underlying demand curve, the reversible option should win.

**What I propose**

Concretely: we spend six weeks instrumenting utilisation properly, rescheduling batch windows away from interactive peaks, and implementing priority-based preemption. We then re-measure. If peak-hour contention persists above a threshold we agree on now, we take a purchase proposal to leadership with real evidence behind it, and I will support it.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be clear that I might be wrong. If our workload grows sharply in the next quarter, or if a customer commitment arrives with hard latency SLAs, the utilisation path becomes a delay rather than a decision, and delay has its own cost. I'd rather accept that risk, which is bounded and visible, than the risk of buying capacity we can't justify, which is neither.

Comments welcome by end of week.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been running hot on our local inference hardware for about six weeks now. Queue times during peak hours have crept from under a second to occasionally eight or ten seconds, and two of our batch pipelines have started missing their windows. The obvious question on the table is whether we should buy another node or figure out how to squeeze more out of the four machines we already own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the answer isn't as simple as "we're at 80% utilization, therefore buy more."

Let's start with the money, since that's where the conversation usually begins. A new node comparable to our existing ones runs roughly $45–55k all-in, plus the ongoing costs of power, cooling, colo space, and — the part we consistently underestimate — the engineering time to integrate, monitor, and maintain it. That's real but not prohibitive for us. The more interesting cost, though, is the opportunity cost of the alternative. If we spend the next six weeks on a serious utilisation effort — better batching, smarter request routing, quantization where the quality tradeoff is acceptable, and killing the two or three internal jobs that run on expensive hardware out of habit rather than necessity — that's six weeks of senior engineer time not spent on the product roadmap. Both options have a price tag. Neither is free.

On latency, the picture is more nuanced than our dashboards suggest. Our p50 latency is fine; the pain is concentrated in the tail, and the tail is driven almost entirely by contention during peak windows. Better scheduling and batching would flatten a lot of that tail without adding any hardware. But there's a floor beyond which software can't help: if demand genuinely exceeds physical capacity for sustained periods, no amount of clever queueing makes the work go faster. My read of our traffic patterns is that we're in the awkward middle — maybe 60% of our peak load is schedulable waste that better software could absorb, and 40% is real demand growth. That ratio is an estimate, not a measurement, and I want to be honest about that.

Reliability is where I think the case for better utilisation actually gets stronger, which is counterintuitive. Right now we run our machines so hot that we have no headroom for failure. If a node goes down, we don't degrade gracefully — we fall off a cliff, and the batch pipelines miss their windows entirely. A utilisation push that brings steady-state load down to 60–65% would give us genuine failover capacity. Buying a fifth node while keeping everything else the same would add capacity but leave us with the same brittle operating pattern, just shifted right. Hardware without operational discipline tends to get consumed by demand growth within a quarter or two anyway.

Then there's reversibility, which I think is the decisive factor. Software improvements are cheap to reverse or adjust — if a batching change causes quality regressions, we roll it back in an afternoon. A hardware purchase is not reversible in any practical sense. We can't return a node after the purchase order clears, and if our demand forecast is wrong — and demand forecasts for AI workloads have been wrong a lot lately, in both directions — we're carrying sunk capital and a higher fixed cost base. There's also model churn to consider: the inference efficiency of the models we serve has improved dramatically over the past year, and there's a reasonable chance that next-generation models will need meaningfully less compute per request, which would strand capacity we bought today.

So my recommendation is this: commit to a focused six-week utilisation effort with explicit, measurable targets — peak p95 latency under two seconds, steady-state utilization at or below 65%, and a documented failover plan that survives one node loss. We should treat that work as a gate, not a substitute. If we hit the targets and demand keeps growing anyway, we buy the node with much better information and a much stronger case, and we'll have the operational maturity to use it well. If we can't hit the targets even with focused effort, that itself is evidence the constraint is physical and the purchase is justified.

The honest uncertainty here is the demand forecast. If a new internal project lands next month and doubles our load overnight, the six weeks of optimisation work will look, in hindsight, like a delay. I accept that risk. The cost of being wrong in that direction is a few weeks of discomfort; the cost of being wrong in the other direction is fifty thousand dollars of stranded hardware and a team that never learned to run lean. I'd rather be wrong the first way.

I'd like to align on this by end of week so we can start the utilisation sprint Monday. Happy to walk through the numbers in detail with anyone who wants to dig in.
